newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong democrats scorn UK, US over backdown.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong democrats scorn UK, US over backdown.

text.p: Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp on Thursday heaped scorn on the United States and Britain for backing off their boycott and deciding to attend the swearing-in of a Beijing-picked legislature.

After British rule ends at midnight next Monday, the new lawmaking body will replace a democratically-elected chamber, throwing out Martin Lee and other popular politicians in favour of several figures rejected by voters in the last elections.

Washington and London, proclaiming cocern over human rights under Chinese rule, had decided to boycott the investiture, but were unable to persuade their allies to follow. In backing down, they cited a practical need to work with the new body.
"I think they are very disgusting and contemptible. But I am not surprised," said legislator Emily Lau, an outspoken voice of democracy in the territory.
"I think people expect the British and American governments to be very weak. If they do this, they just invite contempt.
"They say one thing but refuse to back it up with action... it is a question of consistency, of being responsible for your public statements," she told local radio.
Even some politicians more attuned to Beijing were startled.
"It is baffling to see them blowing, as it were, hot and cold," said Ronald Arculli, a legislator with the usually pro-China Liberal Party.

An editorial in the South China Morning Post, the territory's main English-language newspaper, said Britain and the United States had lost the moral high ground. It accused them of "shilly-shallying edging towards hypocrisy". Opinion polls released on Thursday indicated the new legislature lacked significant public support.
If democratic elections were held now, Lee's Democratic Party would beat pro-Beijing forces hands down and Lee himself would become prime minister, the polls in the South China Morning Post showed.
The job of chief executive goes to Beijing-appointed shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, who on Wednesday unveiled a new honours system rewarding those with "a love for the Motherland".

Among the first to receive the "Grand Bauhinia Medal" -- named after Hong Kong's new floral emblem -- will be Tung's fellow tycoon Henry Fok, who joined a China-backed rescue of his family's troubled shipping empire in the 1980's.

Fok is often described as Hong Kong's new political kingmaker. He made his money running goods into China during a U.N. trade boycott during the Korean war and was labelled a communist sympathiser by British colonial rulers.
The polls also showed that fewer than half of Hong Kong's people supported merger with China, a third favoured independence and 19 percent wanted the British to stay.

The U.S. consul-general in Hong Kong, Richard Boucher, will attend the swearing-in ceremony. It is being boycotted by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who will attend the preceding ceremony officially marking Hong Kong's return to China following 156 years of British rule.

While Prime Minister Tony Blair will stay away, Britain's new consul in the territory, Francis Cornish, and Sir Hugh Davies, head of the Joint Liaison Group monitoring the post-handover period, will now attend the swearing-in.
A Foreign Office spokesman in London stressed: "This in no way implies approval of the provisional legislature to which we are adamantly opposed."

But in Hong Kong the decision was widely seen as Britain's second flip-flop in as many days after bowing to Beijing and agreeing to let armed Chinese troop reinforcements enter Hong Kong just before the handover.
A cartoon in The Hong Kong Standard depicted the United States, Britain and big business trooping into the swearing-in with Martin Lee outside crying: "They're selling us out."
The British commander of Nepalese Gurkhas on Thursday insisted the incoming People's Liberation Army had listened to advice and was determined to succeed.

"The PLA will be just fine," Lieutenant-Colonel Jeremy Ellis, commander of the Queen's Gurkha Signals Regiment, told Reuters. "They are very keen to get it right and have listened to what we say. The key is they want to do well."
The sight of green-uniformed PLA troops revives memories among many Hong Kong people of the 1989 slaughter of unarmed student demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Tung received another boost on Thursday when the colony's top civil servant quashed speculation she would resign.

Chief Secretary Anson Chan, who had earlier hinted she might quit if asked to accept policies that went against her principles, said she had no plans to leave before her scheduled retirement in three years' time.

Chan recently topped a Time Magazine opinion poll as the most popular leader in Hong Kong, ahead of Tung and Lee. Her presence in the post-colonial administration gives it much-needed credibility, and her departure would be a blow to confidence.
